🚨 Every $TAO subnet has been forced to run the same business model. eTAO ends that.

It's one of the biggest changes to subnet economics since dTAO. Watch the 80-second explainer 🎬👇

How it worked until now

Every 12 seconds, each subnet mints new alpha tokens. Almost every subnet split them the exact same way:

• 18% to the owner (the team running it)
• 41% to validators and their stakers (checking the work)
• 41% to miners (doing the work)

A GPU farm, a research lab and a consumer app all lived by one rule.

What eTAO (Expressive TAO) changes

Each subnet owner can now set their own split, within limits:

• Miners: at least 33%
• Validators: up to 50%
• Owners: up to 33% (18% minimum for lease-created subnets)
• Changes about once a week

Total emissions don't change. eTAO only changes where they go.

Why that's a big deal

Different businesses need different budgets:

• A compute subnet short on GPUs pays miners more
• A research team funds its developers through the owner share
• A subnet with hard-to-check work spends more on validators

Targon (SN4) is the live example. In the Talking Targon episode with Const, the team said customers want more compute than it has, and most of it is rented.

Push miners from 41% to 80% and miners get about 95% more tokens. At the same token price, that nearly doubles the budget to bring on GPUs.

More compute → more revenue → bigger buybacks. That's Targon's plan, not a guarantee.

The twist

Lower yield can be bullish.

A high APY tells you how fast new tokens reach stakers. It doesn't tell you what customers pay.

Normal companies make this trade every day: reinvest in production instead of paying out. eTAO lets subnets make the same call.

The guardrails

• Root $TAO stakers are paid their baseline first, calculated from live chain state
• Owners can't set validators below that baseline
• Miners can never drop below a third
• The burn and recycle slots exist but are fixed at zero for now

Why? Const explained it: without a floor, a subnet could cut out its outside holders, fake its price signal and pull emissions it hasn't earned. The floor keeps every subnet paying the network that funds it.

Everything else that just changed

eTAO isn't alone. Bittensor is redesigning itself fast:

• Null Consensus: opt-in, up to 2,500 participant slots per subnet, up from 256
• Proof-of-work registration: miners can join with compute, no TAO upfront
• Subnet registration cost now halves every 8 days, down from 16
• New-subnet immunity drops from 120 days to 60
• Gamma (in development): subnets buy compute, storage and inference from each other with their emissions

Put it together: bigger competitions, easier entry, faster turnover, custom budgets, and soon an internal economy where subnets are each other's customers.

The take

• eTAO is on testnet now. Mainnet comes with the next runtime upgrade (v481)
• An owner can fund the wrong thing. A weak scoring system can pay miners who farm rewards instead of building the product
• Alpha staking yields aren't permanent. A subnet's split is now part of what you're investing in
• Emissions aren't revenue. The bull case only works if extra output gets paid for

Why it matters for AI

AI doesn't grow in straight lines. Agents make thousands of requests while a person reviews one dashboard. Workloads shift from compute to storage to verification in weeks.

A network funding that can't run on one fixed rule.

Now it doesn't have to. 🧠

Sources: Bittensor release notes (v481), Talking Targon Ep. 01 with Const, Novelty Search.

$CLAUDIA is worth paying attention to because it may be more than just a Meme that has attracted Elon's attention.

It could be an early experiment in a new AI-powered IP incubation model, and $HeavyPulp is a valuable case study to reference.

Anabology has already received comments and replies from Elon Musk multiple times. Five interactions in a row suggest that Claudia-related content has not simply appeared on his radar by chance, but has demonstrated an ability to repeatedly capture his attention. That matters.

For most Memes, the hardest part is not launching a token, but finding a source of attention that can be activated repeatedly. Many projects have to keep chasing new trends, riding one person's popularity today and another event tomorrow. Once the external narrative disappears, the community often struggles to keep producing content.

CLAUDIA's potential advantage is that it has an ongoing creative force behind it.

Anabology is not just managing a token. He is trying to use AI to build a virtual character IP that can continue to evolve. This leads me to a more ambitious idea: Could we eventually see a model in which AI autonomously produces high-quality short dramas, continuously creates content around a recurring character, and then uses a token to fund further production?

The short dramas create content, the content attracts attention, the attention flows into the token market, and the fees generated by trading are then used to fund the next round of production. As long as the quality remains high enough, this mechanism could form a positive feedback loop.

The difference from traditional Memes is that the token would no longer be just a symbol waiting to be speculated on. It could become a financing and incentive tool within the content production process.

Of course, this model still needs to be validated in practice, but the potential is clear: if AI can continually lower the cost of producing high-quality content, an IP could generate attention more frequently without relying entirely on the production cycles of the traditional film and television industry.

Claudia provides a useful opportunity to explore this direction.

Elon's repeated interactions are an important attention catalyst in this model. Elon has an enormous reach, and when he repeatedly engages with a creator's work, that content can break out of its original audience. More importantly, when these interactions happen repeatedly, the market starts paying attention to the creator's next release and whether another repost or reply might follow.

This gives Claudia an ongoing series of potential catalysts rather than just a one-time news event.

That is why I believe HeavyPulp is a valuable case study. It demonstrates one possible path: a creator attracts Elon's attention through AI-generated content, a token narrative forms around the creator and their work, and the token is then connected to future content production.

If CLAUDIA can develop along the same path, with Anabology continuously producing content, Elon's interactions amplifying its exposure, and the token mechanism providing funding for further creation, every new release could become another catalyst.

This is why I am paying attention to Anabology's content output. Rather than simply waiting for Elon to reply again, I want to see whether Claudia can continue producing high-quality short videos, establish a recognizable character identity, and gradually attract more creators to participate.

Once Claudia is no longer just Anabology's personal creation but becomes an IP that the community actively wants to expand, its narrative ceiling could rise significantly.

For CLAUDIA, the most promising scenario is not that Elon replies once more and the token rallies again. It is that AI content continues to be produced, Elon's attention amplifies its reach, and the token funds further creation, ultimately forming an attention cycle that can be activated repeatedly.

If this experiment succeeds, CLAUDIA could become more than a Meme dependent on celebrity interactions. It could represent an early attempt at an AI-native content economy.

I will be watching whether Anabology can continue releasing content with strong viral potential and whether token funds can genuinely support future production. If these two elements gradually come together, CLAUDIA's narrative could have much greater staying power than a simple bet on Elon's next reply.

🚨 A Netflix engineer just open-sourced the fix for the most expensive problem in AI: wasted tokens

It's called Headroom, and it might be the smartest fix to high token usage

Your agent reads a 10,000-token log file to find one error.
You paid for all 10,000 tokens.
The answer needed 1,200.

Headroom sits between your agent and the LLM and compresses everything before the model sees it.

JSON, code, logs, RAG chunks, each gets its own specialized compressor.

And it's reversible: the originals stay on your machine, so nothing is lost.

The results speak for themselves:

→ Up to 95% fewer tokens
→ Same accuracy on benchmarks
→ Zero changes to your code

Setup takes one minute:

1. pip install "headroom-ai[all]"
2. headroom wrap claude

Done.

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and anything OpenAI-compatible.

Everything runs locally, fully open source.

The cheapest token is the one you never send.

Andrii and the SOC Prime team have just launched LogTotal and I find the concept quite interesting

You can upload a collection of security logs, run detection rules against the events, correlate the matches into potential attack chains, and use AI to help interpret the results.
What I particularly like is the architecture. Instead of throwing millions of log events at an LLM, it starts with detection rules and correlation, using AI later in the process to help investigate and explain the findings.

Another interesting detail is the approach to privacy. Sensitive identifiers can be pseudonymized locally before uploading the logs. The sanitizer is even available as open source, with a CLI that can run completely offline. So if you don't want to rely on JavaScript delivered by a website, you can inspect the code and sanitize your logs in your own environment before uploading.

Sanitizer: https://t.co/VpMx44CZC7

I think that's a sensible direction for AI-assisted security investigations. It also makes retrospective log analysis accessible without having to set up an entire SIEM infrastructure.

I haven't tested it myself yet, and I'd be more interested in the quality of the detections and correlations than the advertised rule count or processing speed.

But the approach makes sense to me. Definitely worth a closer look.

All of your comments about why my argument is weak revolve around proving consciousness, when my point is about disproving consciousness. 

If someone claims an LLM is conscious, that claim must have testable implications. We can examine its architecture, inspect its mechanisms, run experiments, and test those implications against reality. When they fail, we should discount the premise and/or hypothesis. 

We don’t have to accept consciousness as an explanation simply because someone believes it might exist.

Current LLMs fail to demonstrate many of the characteristics we associate with conscious experience. We definitively know this because humans created them. We understand their architectures, training processes, and inference mechanisms.

So let’s look at a few points, together they provide more than enough evidence to disprove consciousness. 

1. An LLM has no demonstrated subjective awareness of its own existence. No feelings, emotions, or experienced sense of self. What occurs is computation using static weights, context, and mathematical operations.

2. An LLM’s weights don’t learn, grow, or evolve simply because you interact with it. During standard inference, they’re fixed parameters, not a changing dataset. The model doesn’t inherently remember previous API requests. Continuity comes from context history in subsequent requests. The model doesn’t gain experience, it doesn’t remember, it doesn’t learn. It is completely static, read-only, during inference. 

3. Between inference requests, the LLM isn’t thinking. I don’t mean sleeping. I mean there’s no ongoing contemplation, self-reflection, or reconsideration of previous answers. Nothing. The model isn’t sitting around wondering whether it got something wrong or what the meaning of life is, for all practical purposes, it doesn’t exist.

4. These systems were created by people, and much of the underlying technology is open source. You can build your own models, examine implementations, study the architectures, learn how training materials and processes affect how it behaves, and even understand the mathematics behind it. You can see how training produces systems capable of remarkably convincing human-like language and behavior. None of those mechanisms requires consciousness to explain what we’re observing.

5. LLMs are not biological brains. Apples are not oranges, no matter how much you want them to be. Artificial neural networks were inspired in part by biological neuroscience, but their architectures and operating mechanisms are fundamentally different. Similarities in behavior do not establish equivalent internal architectures. 

6. Humans are naturally inclined to recognize life and assume humanity in things that behave like us. We’re social creatures, and anthropomorphism comes naturally. But an LLM isn’t life. It can convincingly emulate feelings, care, and understanding without experiencing any of them. That doesn’t diminish the technology, that is what it was programmed to do.

I appreciate your perspective as a doctor and researcher, but without a solid understanding of LLM architecture and inference, it’s easy to confuse sophisticated emulation with conscious experience.

But don’t fall for it!

I think this (Politico leaking a bad federal bill Anthropic has been pitching) is a really important moment to call on Anthropic to act like it means it:

a) It’s nakedly self-interested for Anthropic to shop around provisions that serve to protect its own wiggle room and its own ability to adjudicate internal and external deployment decisions on Slack (while also publicly warning that its AI might end the world). USG should retain more emergency optionality without having to make an unreasonably detailed affirmative case that predicts whether 50 people will die or 49.

b) I get that Anthropic is worried about model blocking authority being used capriciously. I am too. And maybe this is more about Anthropic’s general distrust of the current admin. Then why preempt states so broadly at the same time? Shouldn’t you *want* California to pass a law that clarifies how and when emergency injunction authority will be used there, and designates it to an expert-staffed authority whose final calls are not arbitrary, but informed by independent embedded evaluators? Shouldn’t you *want* to have more purpose-built tools in our arsenal and not just sledgehammers and export controls?

c) Let’s say this has nothing to do with self-interest at all and reflects a genuinely held belief that it’s time to phase out state-led AI regulation and put Congress in charge, based on some idealized view of what different government actors should and shouldn’t do. I too would love for Congress to pass a strong law that establishes a federal regulator! But given that Congress is still the same dysfunctional Congress it always was, I think the premature preemption view is absurd taken with what Anthropic execs believe about how fast things are moving and how high the stakes are. And it’s definitely absurd taken with the fact that Anthropic is doing plenty of things it wouldn’t do in an ideal world (e.g. racing full steam ahead to RSI), and seems content to ride on its realpolitik estimations of the current landscape of actors there.

Anthropic needs to do better going forward.
